_sweeps.name: Sweep: frontier labs & model releases
_sweeps.rationale: The core capability race between OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, and Meta is the pipeline's primary anchor desk; version releases and benchmark claims move fastest and are least likely to be fully covered by any single feed.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: compute, chips & infrastructure
_sweeps.rationale: Chip generations, foundry capacity, and hyperscaler capex now set the pace of the whole industry as much as model releases do, and this coverage lives mostly in specialist and financial press outside the core AI feeds.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: AI safety, security & alignment
_sweeps.rationale: Safety framework updates, third-party evals (METR, Apollo, UK AISI), and disclosed agentic-AI incidents are distinct from product-release news and are covered by a different set of publishers and government sources.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: policy, regulation & geopolitics
_sweeps.rationale: Binding regulation (EU AI Act enforcement, US state laws, export controls) and US-China dynamics are a standing desk with its own cadence of government and legal-press sources not captured by general tech feeds.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: enterprise adoption, agents & applications
_sweeps.rationale: The shift from chatbots to production agents (coding tools, enterprise platforms, vertical deployments) is where model capability actually meets revenue and is undercovered by pure-research feeds.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: funding, deals & corporate strategy
_sweeps.rationale: Funding rounds, cloud/compute partnerships, and the running capex-bubble debate drive a large share of daily coverage and are reported primarily by business press rather than lab or research feeds.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: open source & research ecosystem
_sweeps.rationale: Open-weight model drops and the academic pipeline (arXiv, NeurIPS/ICML, benchmark leaderboards) move on their own schedule, increasingly led by Chinese labs, and need dedicated discovery beyond arXiv's own feed.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: talent & org dynamics
_sweeps.rationale: High-profile researcher departures, spin-outs, and internal restructurings are a recurring signal of where frontier capability is migrating, and are typically broken by scoop-driven outlets rather than official channels.

_sweeps.name: Sweep: robotics & embodied AI
_sweeps.rationale: Physical/embodied AI is a fast-growing, capital-intensive beat that is genuinely contested as its own desk versus a subset of Enterprise Applications, so it needs explicit discovery rather than incidental pickup.

items.detail: The base noun for the whole beat; almost every story is ultimately about an LLM release, benchmark, or failure mode.
items.name: LLM (Large Language Model)

items.detail: Contested term for human-level general capability; labs (OpenAI, DeepMind) use it in charters/mission statements with no agreed technical definition, so quotes using it should be treated as aspirational/marketing as much as technical.
items.name: AGI (Artificial General Intelligence)

items.detail: Capability beyond AGI; increasingly used by safety-focused writers and by Ilya Sutskever's lab Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI), whose name literalizes the term.
items.name: ASI (Artificial Superintelligence)

items.detail: The standard post-training alignment technique since InstructGPT/ChatGPT; Anthropic's variant using AI-generated feedback against a written 'constitution' instead of human raters is called RLAIF / Constitutional AI (CAI).
items.name: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)

items.detail: Standard architecture pattern for grounding model output in external documents; the acronym collides with the ordinary word 'rag,' so it needs context to disambiguate in text search.
items.name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)

items.detail: Refers both to the prompting technique and to the visible/hidden reasoning traces that 'reasoning models' (o-series, Claude extended thinking, Gemini 'Thinking') generate before an answer.
items.name: CoT (Chain of Thought)

items.detail: Sparse-activation architecture used by GPT-4-class, Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, and Grok models; commonly discussed via 'active vs. total parameters.'
items.name: MoE (Mixture of Experts)

items.detail: The instruction-tuning stage before preference optimization; usually mentioned alongside RLHF/DPO in model/system cards' training pipeline description.
items.name: SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning)

items.detail: Simpler alternative to PPO-based RLHF that optimizes directly on preference pairs; widely adopted by open-model fine-tuners since 2023.
items.name: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)

items.detail: The two dominant reinforcement-learning algorithms in the space: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) is the original Schulman-era OpenAI technique behind classic RLHF; GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), popularized by DeepSeek's R1 paper, is the cheaper alternative now widely used for reasoning-model training.
items.name: PPO / GRPO

items.detail: Anthropic's open standard (Nov 2024) for connecting LLM apps/agents to external tools and data; the acronym is otherwise overloaded (e.g., 'master control program'), so confirm context in general text.
items.name: MCP (Model Context Protocol)

items.detail: Ubiquitous shorthand in benchmark reporting; watch for 'SOTA' claims that quietly mean 'best on one cherry-picked eval.'
items.name: SOTA (State of the Art)

items.detail: The 2024-26 shift toward spending more compute at answer-generation time (reasoning models) rather than only at training time; core to the o1/o3, Claude 'thinking,' and Gemini 'Thinking' narrative.
items.name: Test-time compute / TTC / inference-time scaling

items.detail: Standard label for multimodal image+text models (e.g., GPT-4V lineage, Gemini, Claude with vision); often used loosely to mean any multimodal model.
items.name: VLM (Vision-Language Model)

items.detail: The memory technology (HBM3e, HBM4) that is often the actual bottleneck in AI-chip supply stories, not raw compute.
items.name: HBM (High Bandwidth Memory)

items.detail: Nvidia's proprietary parallel-compute software platform; the 'CUDA moat' is standard shorthand for Nvidia's software lock-in versus AMD/TPU/custom silicon.
items.name: CUDA

items.detail: Floating-point operations per second is the standard compute unit; training runs are often sized in total FLOPs and compared against export-control thresholds defined in FLOPs.
items.name: FLOP/s and exaFLOP/petaFLOP

items.detail: Ambiguous capitalization collision: lowercase-x 'xAI' is Elon Musk's company (maker of Grok, folded into what is now sometimes branded SpaceXAI as of early 2026); capital-X 'XAI' is the unrelated academic field of explainable AI.
items.name: xAI vs. XAI

items.detail: Anthropic's model family, named after Claude Shannon; also just a common first name, so 'Claude' needs entity-linking care in text (Claude Opus, Sonnet, Haiku tiers).
items.name: Claude

items.detail: Google DeepMind's flagship model family; also NASA's 1960s Gemini program and the zodiac sign, both of which surface as false-positive matches in naive text search.
items.name: Gemini

items.detail: xAI's chatbot/model family; the word predates the company by decades as SF slang (from Heinlein's 'Stranger in a Strange Land') meaning to understand deeply — a common false-positive source.
items.name: Grok

items.detail: Meta's open-weight model family (Llama 2/3/4); collides constantly with the animal in generic text.
items.name: Llama

items.detail: Both the French AI lab and its flagship model line; also a Mediterranean wind and a historic French fighter jet, so disambiguation depends heavily on surrounding context.
items.name: Mistral

items.detail: Google's original ChatGPT-competitor chatbot (2023), later rebranded to Gemini; still appears in older sources and retrospectives, and is a common English word (poet) otherwise.
items.name: Bard

items.detail: Anthropic's naming convention for Claude's capability tiers (largest to smallest); each name is also an ordinary literary/musical-form word, requiring context to read as a Claude model reference.
items.name: Opus / Sonnet / Haiku

items.detail: Amazon's in-house foundation model family (Amazon Nova); also a generic astronomy term and used as a product name across many unrelated companies.
items.name: Nova

items.detail: Microsoft Research's small/efficient language model family; collides with the Greek letter used constantly in math/ML notation.
items.name: Phi

items.detail: Open-weight model family from UAE's Technology Innovation Institute (TII); also the bird, and shares a name with unrelated 'Falcon' products/rockets in other industries.
items.name: Falcon

items.detail: Alibaba Cloud's open-weight model family, one of the most widely used bases for Chinese and open-source fine-tunes.
items.name: Qwen

items.detail: Chinese AI lab and its eponymous model family (DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1); the company name and model name are used near-interchangeably in coverage, which can blur lab-vs-model references.
items.name: DeepSeek

items.detail: Microsoft's branded product line (GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Copilot); also drifted into generic industry usage as a synonym for any AI coding/work assistant, so 'a copilot' vs. 'Copilot' the product need distinguishing.
items.name: Copilot

items.detail: OpenAI's text/image-to-video model; a common Japanese given name and word ('sky'), so context matters for disambiguation.
items.name: Sora

items.detail: DeepMind's recognizable 'Alpha-' naming convention for landmark research systems (games, protein folding, math, code); good signal that a story is about DeepMind-lineage research rather than product releases.
items.name: AlphaGo / AlphaFold / AlphaZero / AlphaCode / AlphaProof

items.detail: OpenAI's 2025 open-weight model release, whose name embeds the ambiguous acronym OSS (open-source software) even though the license is 'open weights,' not full open source in the traditional sense.
items.name: gpt-oss

items.detail: A load-bearing distinction the industry is sloppy about: 'open weights' (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, gpt-oss) means downloadable parameters under a license, not necessarily open training data/code, unlike strict open-source definitions.
items.name: Open weights vs. open source

items.detail: Lab-specific voluntary safety-scaling policies: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (with ASL-1 through ASL-4 AI Safety Levels), OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework — same concept, different names per lab, frequently confused.
items.name: RSP / Preparedness Framework / Frontier Safety Framework

items.detail: The crowdsourced head-to-head model ranking (formerly LMSYS Chatbot Arena, now under the LMArena org) that reports rankings as chess-style Elo scores; a widely cited but contested proxy for 'best model.'
items.name: Chatbot Arena / LMSYS / Elo

items.detail: The recurring benchmark-name shorthand set: MMLU (broad knowledge), GPQA (graduate-level science Q&A), SWE-bench (real-world software-engineering tasks, often cited as 'SWE-bench Verified'), and ARC-AGI (abstraction/reasoning, positioned as an AGI-adjacent test resistant to memorization).
items.name: MMLU / GPQA / SWE-bench / ARC-AGI

items.detail: The recurring safety-vocabulary cluster: 'jailbreak' for adversarial prompts that bypass safety training, 'red-teaming' for structured adversarial testing before release, 'guardrails' for runtime safety filters, and 'hallucination' for confidently fabricated output.
items.name: Jailbreak / red-teaming / guardrails / hallucination

items.detail: Nvidia's architecture codenames (Hopper = H100/H200, Blackwell = B200/GB200/GB300) recur constantly in compute-supply reporting; 'Grace' is Nvidia's CPU (Grace Hopper / Grace Blackwell Superchip), which shares its name with computing pioneer Grace Hopper — itself the source of the Hopper codename.
items.name: Chip codename generations: Hopper / Blackwell / Grace

jargon.summary: AI-industry writing runs on a dense, fast-turning stack of acronyms (LLM, RLHF, RAG, MoE, MCP), lab-specific safety-policy names that all mean roughly the same thing (RSP, Preparedness Framework, Frontier Safety Framework), and — distinctively for this domain — a habit of naming flagship models after ordinary short words (Claude, Gemini, Grok, Llama, Mistral, Nova, Phi, Falcon, Sonnet, Opus) that collide constantly with their non-AI meanings in text. A second layer of ambiguity comes from acronym overload, where the same short string means different things depending on context (xAI the company vs. XAI the research field; MCP the Anthropic protocol vs. other uses; RAG the technique vs. the word 'rag'). A third layer is fast-moving technical shorthand for training methods (SFT, DPO, PPO/GRPO), hardware generations (H100/B200, Hopper/Blackwell, HBM, CUDA), and benchmarks (MMLU, SWE-bench, ARC-AGI, Chatbot Arena/Elo) that insiders use as compressed signals of capability and provenance. Getting these canonical — distinguishing the model from the company, the codename from the chip, the acronym from its homonym — is what keeps downstream entity extraction from silently corrupting.

items.detail: Alphabet's unified AI research and product lab (merger of Google Brain and DeepMind, completed 2023), builder of the Gemini model family and TPU-adjacent research.

items.detail: Elon Musk's AI lab, builder of the Grok model family, now merged with X (Twitter) under Musk's holding structure; experienced high-profile leadership departures in early 2026.
items.name: xAI

items.detail: Meta Platforms' AI division, historically known for open-weight Llama releases and FAIR (Fundamental AI Research); restructured into Meta Superintelligence Labs amid a stalled flagship model in 2026.

items.detail: Paris-based frontier lab and Europe's leading open-weight and commercial model builder (Mistral Large/Medium/Small families), positioned as the EU's sovereign-AI champion.

items.detail: Hangzhou-based Chinese lab (High-Flyer-backed) whose efficient open-weight DeepSeek-V3/R1 releases reset assumptions about training cost and triggered market-wide reaction in early 2025.

items.detail: US government standards body; its AI Safety Institute was renamed the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in 2025, shifting emphasis toward standards, security, and countering foreign over-regulation rather than broad safety framing.
items.name: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) / CAISI

items.detail: UK government body (formerly named the AI Safety Institute; renamed AI Security Institute in Feb 2025) that evaluates frontier models for national-security-relevant risks; publishes active technical safety research.

items.detail: European Commission body that both develops guidance and enforces the EU AI Act's general-purpose-AI obligations; high-risk obligations began applying broadly from August 2026.

items.detail: Coalition of national AI safety/security institutes (US, UK, EU, Japan, Canada, Australia, Singapore, Korea, and others) launched from the 2023 Bletchley Summit process to coordinate frontier-model evaluation.

items.detail: OECD's AI policy arm; author of the widely cited OECD AI Principles, which underpin much subsequent national and international AI governance vocabulary.

items.detail: The FTC is the primary US enforcement agency for AI-related consumer-protection and competition actions absent comprehensive federal AI legislation; California has become a de facto US AI regulator via state law requiring frontier-developer transparency and safety disclosures.

items.detail: China's primary AI/internet regulator, responsible for generative-AI service approvals and content/algorithm registration requirements that all Chinese labs must clear before public release.

items.detail: Berkeley-based nonprofit that runs independent capability and dangerous-capability evaluations on frontier models pre-deployment, frequently cited in lab system cards and government assessments.

items.detail: Nonprofit research group tracking compute trends, training-run scale, and model benchmarking data; a widely cited independent data source for the pace of frontier AI progress.

items.detail: AI safety organization specializing in evaluating models for deceptive alignment and 'scheming' behavior; has published joint findings with OpenAI on this topic.
items.name: Apollo Research

items.detail: The oldest dedicated AI safety research organization (est. 2000), focused on theoretical alignment and existential-risk research rather than empirical evaluation.

items.detail: Nonprofit behind the widely signed 2023 'statement on AI risk' and ongoing work on benchmarks and AI policy advocacy.

items.detail: Seattle nonprofit research lab (founded by Paul Allen) producing fully open models, datasets, and benchmarks (OLMo series); a leading source of open-science alternatives to closed frontier labs.

items.detail: Grassroots nonprofit open-research collective (GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, Pythia, the Pile dataset); smaller-budget peer to Ai2 in the open-research ecosystem.

items.detail: Academic policy and research hub best known for the annual AI Index Report, a widely cited benchmark-of-record for industry-wide trends.

items.detail: Montreal-based academic AI research institute (associated with Yoshua Bengio), a leading center for deep learning research and AI-safety-adjacent policy work.
items.name: Mila – Quebec AI Institute

items.detail: Leading venture capital firm with a dedicated AI investment strategy; among the most active backers of foundation-model and applied-AI startups.
items.name: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z)

items.detail: Major venture firm with sustained frontier-model and applied-AI investments; participates alongside sovereign wealth funds in mega-rounds.

items.detail: Japanese conglomerate and major OpenAI investor/compute-infrastructure partner (Stargate project), representative of sovereign-scale capital entering frontier AI.
items.name: SoftBank Group

items.name: MGX / Gulf sovereign wealth funds (e.g., PIF, Mubadala)

organizations.summary: The organizations facet spans five clusters a daily reader meets constantly: (1) frontier builders — a small set of labs (US, and increasingly Chinese) shipping the models that set the pace; (2) infrastructure — chipmakers, foundries, and hyperscaler clouds whose supply constraints and capex now drive the news cycle as much as model releases; (3) capital — the VC firms and sovereign wealth vehicles writing the mega-rounds that fund frontier training runs; (4) governance — the patchwork of national institutes, regulators, and standards bodies now moving from voluntary frameworks to binding enforcement (EU AI Act enforcement began August 2026); (5) research and evaluation — nonprofits, academic labs, and open-source collectives that produce the benchmarks, safety evals, and open-weight alternatives the rest of the ecosystem cites. Corporate structures matter here (OpenAI's nonprofit/PBC split, Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, Google DeepMind's absorption into Alphabet) and several entities have recently renamed or repositioned (UK AISI → AI Security Institute; US AISI → CAISI), so canonical current names are flagged where a rename occurred.

items.detail: Anthropic's model family; as of mid-2026 the lineup is Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5 and a new top tier, Fable 5 (released July 2026), with Sonnet/Opus/Fable at 1M-token context.

items.detail: Nvidia's parallel-computing software platform/API, the foundational lock-in layer underlying essentially all Nvidia AI hardware coverage; also anchors the DGX system line and NIM inference microservices.

items.detail: Mistral AI's flagship 675B-parameter model (December 2025), Apache 2.0 licensed; the family also spans Medium 3.5, Small 4 and the Ministral 3 edge models (14B/8B/3B), plus specialist models like Voxtral speech and an enterprise custom-training product, Forge.

items.name: METR

products.summary: The "products" facet in AI-industry press coverage spans five overlapping clusters. First, frontier foundation-model families from the labs (Claude, GPT-5.x/ChatGPT, Gemini 3, Grok, Mistral Large, Llama 4) plus the fast-moving Chinese open-weight tier (DeepSeek, Qwen, and their peers Kimi and GLM), each iterated frequently enough that version numbers themselves become news. Second, the compute-hardware layer that press treats as a product race in its own right: Nvidia's Blackwell-to-Rubin GPU transition plus its CUDA/NIM software stack, and the hyperscaler-custom-silicon response (Google TPU/Ironwood, AWS Trainium, AMD Instinct, plus specialist inference chipmakers Cerebras and Groq). Third, the applied-product layer built on those models: agentic coding tools (Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex), enterprise agent platforms (Microsoft Foundry/Copilot, Salesforce Agentforce, Palantir AIP, Amazon Bedrock/Alexa+), and generative media tools (Sora, Veo, Midjourney, Runway, ElevenLabs, Suno). Fourth, physical/embodied AI, dominated by humanoid-robot programs (Figure, Tesla Optimus, 1X) now treated as a distinct beat. Fifth, the infrastructure/measurement substrate the press relies on to make capability claims legible: open-model hubs and serving frameworks (Hugging Face, vLLM), evaluation benchmarks (SWE-bench), independent evaluators (METR, Epoch AI), and megaproject infrastructure like OpenAI's Stargate. Naming is volatile -- version suffixes (4.6, V4, 3.5 Flash) and rebrands (Windsurf→Devin Desktop, Azure AI Foundry→Microsoft Foundry) shift within months, so a pipeline should track family names as the stable anchor and treat specific version strings as time-stamped attributes.

publications.summary: AI-industry trade press splits into three layers a serious reader triangulates daily: (1) official lab/vendor channels (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, Mistral, Meta, Microsoft Research, Hugging Face, xAI, Cohere) for primary announcements, where RSS support is inconsistent -- OpenAI and DeepMind publish clean feeds, Anthropic and Mistral notably do not, forcing reliance on community-maintained scrapers; (2) broad tech-business outlets with dedicated AI verticals (TechCrunch, Ars Technica, VentureBeat, MIT Technology Review, WIRED, The Information, 404 Media, Platformer, Axios), most of which do carry AI-specific RSS feeds, though top-tier subscription outlets like The Information withhold feeds behind paywalls; and (3) independent insider newsletters written by practitioners and researchers (Import AI, The Batch, Interconnects, Don't Worry About the Vase, AI as Normal Technology, Simon Willison, Latent Space, Ben's Bites, TLDR AI), almost all Substack-hosted with standard feed conventions. A fourth, adjacent layer is raw research signal -- arXiv's cs.AI feed and Hugging Face's Daily Papers -- which the trade press itself draws from; Papers with Code, once a staple here, was retired by Meta in mid-2025. Feed URLs for smaller/independent newsletters were confirmed via search but not all were independently fetched, so treat any marked 'unconfirmed' as needing a live check before wiring into the pipeline.

items.detail: Tracks flagship model launches and capability leapfrogging among Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT/o-series), Google DeepMind (Gemini), Mistral AI, xAI (Grok), Meta (Llama), and fast-rising Chinese labs like DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen), and Moonshot AI (Kimi).

items.detail: Covers the physical substrate of the industry: Nvidia's GPU generations (Blackwell, Rubin) and rivals like AMD and Google's TPUs, hyperscaler capex from Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, data-center buildouts, power/energy bottlenecks, and sovereign-compute programs; SemiAnalysis is a widely-cited trade source here.

items.detail: Follows interpretability research, red-teaming and model evals, frontier safety frameworks such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy and OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, government safety institutes (UK AISI, US CAISI at NIST), and disclosed agentic-AI security incidents.
items.name: AI Safety, Security & Alignment

items.detail: Spans EU AI Act implementation, US federal/state AI rulemaking and executive orders, US-China export controls on advanced chips, and the international AI summit track (Bletchley/Seoul/Paris/India 'AI Action Summit' series).
items.name: Policy, Regulation & Geopolitics

items.detail: Covers agentic AI moving into production (coding agents, browser/computer-use agents), enterprise platforms like Microsoft Copilot and Salesforce Agentforce, and coding tools such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code, plus vertical deployments in healthcare, legal and finance.
items.name: Enterprise Adoption, Agents & Applications

items.detail: Tracks mega VC rounds and valuations, compute-supply and cloud partnerships (e.g. Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon/Google-Anthropic), M&A and lab acquihires, IPO speculation (CoreWeave and peers), and the running 'AI capex bubble' debate among analysts and investors.
items.name: Funding, Deals & Corporate Strategy

items.detail: Follows open-weight model drops (Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen), the academic pipeline via arXiv and venues like NeurIPS and ICML, and benchmark/leaderboard activity (MMLU, GPQA, SWE-bench, LMArena) often surfaced through Hugging Face.
items.name: Open Source & Research Ecosystem

items.detail: Covers high-profile researcher moves, lab spin-outs (Safe Superintelligence, Thinking Machines Lab), compensation wars for AI talent, and internal restructurings or leadership shakeups at major labs.

items.detail: Covers humanoid and embodied-AI efforts such as Figure AI, Tesla Optimus, and Boston Dynamics, plus robot foundation/world-model research, an area of rapidly growing capital and lab attention but still adjacent to the core software-model beat.
items.name: Robotics & Embodied AI

themes.summary: In AI-industry intelligence, "themes" are the standing desks a daily brief organizes around rather than one-off stories: who's shipping frontier models, who's building the compute to train and serve them, whether those systems are safe and secure, how governments are regulating and geopoliticizing them, how businesses are actually deploying them (increasingly as agents), where the money is flowing, what the open-source/research community is doing, who's moving between labs, and — as a newer, fast-growing beat — physical/embodied AI. These desks overlap constantly in practice (a chip export-control story is both Compute and Policy; an agent security breach is both Safety and Enterprise), and the boundary of a ninth desk like Robotics is genuinely contested as of late 2026 — some newsrooms fold it into Enterprise Applications rather than staffing it separately. The five operator-hinted entities (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, Mistral) map respectively onto Frontier Labs, Frontier Labs, Frontier Labs, Compute/Infrastructure, and Frontier Labs/open-weight coverage, confirming those as anchor desks.
